data.title: Middle East Eye: Three Palestinians injured in Israeli drone attacks on Gaza
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Three Palestinians injured in Israeli drone attacks on Gaza
Two Palestinians were injured, one critically, on Sunday morning after an Israeli drone targeted a group of Palestinians in Al-Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, Wafa reported.
Another Palestinian was injured when an Israeli drone struck near tents sheltering displaced Palestinians in the vicinity of Sheikh Radwan Market, north of Gaza City.
The report said that Israeli forces also shelled areas south of Khan Younis and opened fire from military vehicles east of the city. At the same time, artillery shelling and heavy gunfire targeted the Mawasi Rafah area in the southern Gaza Strip.
Israeli military helicopters also opened heavy fire east of Gaza City, while tanks and naval vessels fired toward the northwestern areas of the city, according to Wafa.
In the occupied West Bank, meanwhile, Wafa reported that Israeli forces tightened restrictions by closing the gate at the entrance to the town of Turmus Ayya, north of Ramallah, and “harassed citizens”.
They also closed the entrances to villages such as Aboud, Nabi Saleh, Atara and Taybeh and set up a military checkpoint at the entrance to Yabroud and Ein Sinya, the report said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iraq seeks US exemption from sanctions on Iranian airlines
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Iraq seeks US exemption from sanctions on Iranian airlines
The Iraqi government has said it is in talks with the United States to seek an exemption from sanctions on Iranian airlines, which have disrupted travel for patients, students and pilgrims.
All Iraqi airports enforced the US ban this week, resulting in major disruption at the airport serving the holy city of Najaf, the main destination in Iraq for Iranian flights.
"The Iraqi government is holding direct talks with the American side to exempt certain Iraqi airports from these measures," the prime minister's media office said.
An exemption, it added, would allow flights to resume "for humanitarian reasons, including medical treatment, education, religious visits, and for the interest of civilians".
Iranian airlines mainly carry Iraqi Shia pilgrims to Iran's holy cities or Iranians visiting sacred sites in Iraq. The flights also serve Iraqi students studying in Iran and patients seeking medical treatment there.
In an interview with Iranian news agency ISNA, Iran's ambassador to Iraq Mohammad Kazem Al-Sadegh said his country was also in contact with authorities in Baghdad to find a way to restore the flights.
"There are roughly 25 daily flights from Iran to Najaf and about 15 flights to Baghdad, and... around 12,000 to 13,000 people travel between Iran and Iraq and vice versa on Iranian airlines, which is not a small number," he said.
Report by AFP

data.title: Middle East Eye: Morning recap
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Morning recap
Good morning Middle East Eye readers,
If you're just joining us, here are key developments from across the region:
• Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that Tehran had seen an initial reaction from US President Donald Trump to its proposal but had yet to receive an official response through mediators.
• Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has said that Iran no longer trusts negotiations with the United States after previous rounds of talks were followed by attacks and sanctions.
• The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has warned it will attack US warships, even those in the Indian Ocean, if Washington launches new attacks against Iran.
• Israeli forces shot at and injured a Palestinian girl early on Sunday at the Qalandia military checkpoint, north of occupied Jerusalem.
• Parents across Riyadh received emails from schools on Sunday announcing a last-minute plan to shift to remote learning for a week.
• Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has called on Israel to “go to war” in the occupied West Bank and “do what we did in Gaza”.
• The Israeli army has carried out “violent explosions” in the vicinity of Khiam, a town along Lebanon's southern border with Israel.
• An Israeli air strike on a tent in the Sheikh Radwan neighbourhood of northern Gaza City has injured several displaced people.
• Israel’s attorney general has ordered a one-month postponement of an E1 settlement construction tender in the occupied West Bank to avoid it being used for electioneering.
• US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has thanked the governments of the United Kingdom, Turkey, Oman and the UAE for supporting Washington's "Operation Economic Outcast", a harsh economic campaign against Iran.
• Hundreds of pro-Palestine protesters marched on Labour's annual conference, the first after Andy Burnham took over as prime minister, in Liverpool and called for an end to UK arms sales to Israel.

data.title: Middle East Eye: 'I'm a man of strong faith,' says Irish goalkeeper after withdrawing from Israel match
data.author: Qazi Zaid
data.summary:
'I'm a man of strong faith,' says Irish goalkeeper after withdrawing from Israel match
Republic of Ireland goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu has withdrawn from the team’s Nations League match against Israel, saying his decision was based on his opposition to the killing of civilians.
“My decision is based purely on the belief the killing of innocent people is wrong,” Bazunu said in a statement posted on social media.
“Representing my country means everything to me,” Bazunu wrote. “I am a man of strong faith and try my best to be a person of morals and principles, therefore I feel that participating in the upcoming matches against Israel would be wrong.”
He added: “There are times when you have the opportunity to stand for a greater cause, and I strongly believe this is one of those moments.”
The Republic of Ireland will nevertheless play Israel in Sunday's Uefa Nations League match in Debrecen, Hungary, after the squad voted by a significant majority to proceed with the fixture, Football Association of Ireland CEO David Courell said on Saturday.
The vote followed several hours of discussions at the team hotel over whether to boycott the game.
Ireland will wear black armbands during the match and will not shake hands with the Israeli players before kickoff, according to the report.

data.title: Middle East Eye: 'Do there what we did in Gaza': Smotrich calls for full-scale war in occupied West Bank
data.author: Qazi Zaid
data.summary:
'Do there what we did in Gaza': Smotrich calls for full-scale war in occupied West Bank
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has called for Israel to “go to war” in the occupied West Bank and “do there what we did in Gaza”, as the country heads towards general elections next month.
Smotrich, the leader of the far-right Religious Zionism party, in an interview with Ynet’s 120 and One political podcast, also reasserted his demand for dismantling the Palestinian Authority, which exercises limited self-rule in parts of the occupied West Bank.
The call for a full-scale Israeli war comes amid relentless settler violence and movement restrictions across the West Bank.
On Sunday, Israeli authorities ordered a "comprehensive closure" of the crossings into the occupied territory for the Jewish holiday of Sukkot.
Israeli forces tightened restrictions around the West Bank city of Ramallah, closing roads and entrances to several towns and villages, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Local sources told Wafa that the entrance gate to Turmus Ayya, north of Ramallah, was closed and residents were “harassed”.
Wafa also reported that entrances to Aboud, Nabi Saleh, Atara and Taybeh were closed, while military checkpoints were set up at the entrances to Yabroud and Ein Sinyah.
Smotrich, who is a leading advocate of expanding illegal Israeli settlements and extending Israeli sovereignty over the occupied West Bank, also defended his wider political agenda ahead of the 27 October elections.

data.title: Middle East Eye: US-led Board of Peace says Unrwa will have no role in Gaza
data.author: Qazi Zaid
data.summary:
US-led Board of Peace says Unrwa will have no role in Gaza
The US-led Board of Peace has said the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, Unrwa, will have no role in Gaza, echoing a longstanding Israeli demand to sideline the organisation.
The board, which has been tasked with overseeing the Gaza ceasefire and reconstruction, said it would work only with partners it considers “reliable” and capable of meeting the needs of Gaza’s population.
It added that Unrwa does not meet that standard.
The decision comes days after the board unveiled a multibillion-dollar plan to begin rebuilding Gaza, following years of Israeli military operations that have devastated the territory.
Hamas has criticised the board’s decision to exclude Unrwa, which provides education, health care and other services to millions of Palestinian refugees.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Recap: Iran says war with US not over
data.author: Qazi Zaid
data.summary:
Recap: Iran says war with US not over
Iran and the United States remain at odds over the Strait of Hormuz after President Donald Trump rejected Tehran’s proposal to reopen the waterway. Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran was still waiting for an official response through mediators and would not abandon its conditions for reopening the strait.
Iran’s army chief, General Amir Hatami, meanwhile said the war was not over and that Tehran needed to consolidate what he called its victory, while Iranian officials have threatened attacks on US ships in the Indian Ocean if a new war breaks out.
Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while Tehran says the waterway will remain closed until its conditions are met.
Tehran says any renewed US attack could trigger a response involving new military technologies and previously unused targets.
The IRGC says it captured a US Remus 600 autonomous underwater vehicle in the Strait of Hormuz.
Israeli attacks continue in Gaza, while Israeli forces have also carried out air and artillery strikes in southern Lebanon.
Yemeni government forces have launched operations against Houthi positions in Taiz as the conflict continues to displace civilians.

data.title: Middle East Eye: In Egypt, leaving prison does not mean escaping the security state
data.author: Asim Qureshi
data.summary:
In Egypt, leaving prison does not mean escaping the security state
Submitted by
Asim Qureshi
on
Sun, 09/27/2026 - 15:09
Abdelrahman ElGendy's memoir Huna shows how release from an Egyptian prison brings surveillance, enforced silence and the threat of renewed detention
Security forces guard Cairo's Tora prison, one of several in which Abdelrahman ElGendy was held over six years of detention, on 17 June 2019 (Reuters/Amr Abdallah Dalsh)
Off
From the very beginning of his detention, Abdelrahman ElGendy, who had just turned 17, was forced to reckon with the constant assault that is prison life in Egypt.
After being unlawfully detained in October 2013 for being close to a protest, and categorised as an alleged Muslim Brotherhood "terrorist" (read: protester), he found himself interned in Egypt's spiralling archipelago of political prisons, along with his father.
The assault that is prison life is not just in the physical act of detention, or the violence and torture enacted by captors; it is in every sound and movement made in the prison. Contrary to popular understanding, an assault in law is not an act of violence itself, but the apprehension that unlawful violence might take place - and nothing better describes life in Egypt's prisons than a constant assault.
On his first night, given no actual reason for his arrest other than the amorphous accusation of being Ikhwan (Muslim Brotherhood), ElGendy recalls in his memoir, Huna :
"Are they going to torture us?" I blurted. I could not look at Baba.
"Well, they haven't so far. So that's a good sign." Aboulfetouh shrugged. "Maybe they'll pass us tonight."
Ten minutes later, the locks clanked outside, and I stiffened. The guard pushed open the door and signaled to me and Baba to follow him.
They came for us.
